Name: Hanno’s Periplus
Metaphysical Tags: Phenomenology (Experiential), Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Clockwork (Causal Determinism)
Arts and Sciences Tags: Biology, Political Science / Law, Economics, History, Anthropology
Short Description: A Carthaginian maritime account describing Hanno’s state-sponsored expedition beyond the Pillars of Heracles and along the Atlantic coast of northwestern Africa. The surviving Greek text reports the foundation of several settlements, encounters with coastal peoples and landscapes, and the dedication of the expedition’s record in the sanctuary of Kronos at Carthage, conventionally associated with Baal Hammon. It presents itself as a Greek rendering of a Punic inscription, although the date of the voyage, the extent of later compression, and the relationship between the surviving version and any Punic original remain debated.

Name: Kition Inscriptions
Metaphysical Tags: Becoming (Process Ontology), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: A broad corpus of Phoenician inscriptions from Kition on Cyprus, ranging from an early dedication to Astarte to royal, administrative, funerary, and votive texts. Written principally in Phoenician, with Greek also appearing in the city’s later epigraphic environment, the inscriptions document the institutions, lineages, cults, and political life of a major Phoenician-ruled Cypriot kingdom. Their inclusion here represents the eastern Phoenician background and wider network from which Punic culture developed, rather than a directly Carthaginian corpus.

Name: Tophet Inscriptions
Metaphysical Tags: Apophatic–Aporetic (Unknowable), Phenomenology (Experiential), Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Grid (Systematic Structuralism)
Short Description: Short Punic votive inscriptions carved on stelae from the tophet precinct at Carthage and related western Phoenician sites. They commonly dedicate an offering to Tanit and Baal Hammon in fulfillment of a vow, using formulas that state that the deity heard and blessed the dedicator. The stelae stood over urns containing cremated remains of very young children and, in some cases, animals. Although the precise interpretation and scale remain debated, the combined epigraphic, archaeological, and literary evidence makes it highly likely that a substantial number of the children were intentionally offered in sacrifice. The inscriptions reveal a tightly organized ritual system centered on vows, costly offerings, divine reciprocity, and family devotion.

Name: Punic Curse Tablets
Metaphysical Tags: Becoming (Process Ontology), Dialectics (Conflict), Subversion (Negation), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: A very small pre-Roman corpus of Punic lead curse texts from Carthage, represented above all by the well-preserved tablet KAI 89. KAI 89 appeals to the deity Ḥawwat in response to the theft of silver, binding the missing property to the goddess and calling for judgment against the unknown offender. The tablet was deposited in a funerary setting, linking the written imprecation to ritual authority and the world of the dead. It provides rare evidence that Punic speakers used written theft curses before the Roman destruction of Carthage, while the much larger curse-tablet corpus from the city belongs to the later Roman period.

Name: Carthaginian Agricultural Treatise
Metaphysical Tags: Becoming (Process Ontology), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Dialectics (Conflict)
Short Description: A lost Punic agricultural encyclopedia in twenty-eight books attributed to Mago of Carthage. It treated estate management, soils, grain and fruit cultivation, viticulture, animal husbandry, veterinary practice, and food preservation, combining practical observation with the accumulated farming knowledge of Punic North Africa. After Carthage was destroyed in 146 BCE, the Roman Senate ordered the work translated into Latin by Decimus Junius Silanus; Greek adaptations and quotations in Varro, Columella, Pliny the Elder, and other agronomists preserve fragments of its contents. Mago’s own date is uncertain, so the third-century placement is approximate.

Name: Marseille Tariff
Short Description: A Punic sacrificial tariff carved on limestone, probably produced at Carthage but discovered reused in Marseille in 1845. The surviving twenty-one lines regulate priestly fees and the division of meat and other offerings for different classes of sacrifice, including cattle, sheep, goats, birds, oil, milk, and grain products. Its language and structure closely parallel a fragmentary tariff found at Carthage, and the opening refers to a sanctuary of Baal-Saphon. Rather than documenting a Phoenician community at Massalia, the stone was most likely transported there from Carthage, perhaps as ship ballast. The inscription offers unusually concrete evidence for the legal and economic administration of Punic temple ritual.

Name: Cippi of Melqart
Short Description: A pair of marble cippi bearing parallel Phoenician and Greek votive inscriptions. The brothers Abdosir and Osirshamar, identified in Greek as Dionysios and Serapion, dedicated them to Melqart; the Greek text renders the god as Heracles. The paired inscriptions show how Phoenician religious identity could be expressed through a Hellenistic bilingual form in Punic Malta. In 1758, Jean-Jacques Barthélemy used the bilingual text as a major key in the decipherment of Phoenician. One cippus is held in Valletta and the other in the Louvre.
